learn.hook: Imagine a group of families settling beside a river, clearing land and calling it home. That's how a janapada began!
points: After the great Harappan cities declined (after about 1900 BCE), people in northern India lived mostly in villages for many centuries.
The Vedas are the oldest texts of India. The Rigveda is the oldest of the four Vedas (Rig, Sama, Yajur and Atharva). They tell us about the life, beliefs and prayers of the people who composed them.
A 'jana' was a people or clan. 'Janapada' means 'the place where a jana set its foot', that is, a territory where a people settled.
Janapadas had their own rulers or councils. Early Vedic texts mention assemblies called the sabhā and the samiti where important matters were discussed.
Over time, some janapadas grew larger and stronger by adding land, people and wealth.

example.q: A word is made of 'jana' (people) and 'pada' (foot). Why is 'janapada' a good name for a settled territory?
steps: 'Pada' means foot, so 'janapada' is where the people placed their foot.
Placing one's foot somewhere suggests settling down in that place.
So the word describes land where a people settled.
example.answer: Because it means 'the land where a people set foot and settled'.

learn.reallife: Many Indian place names still keep old meanings; studying such words is one way historians learn about the past.

games.title: True or false: early states
items: The Rigveda is the oldest of the four Vedas.
It is the earliest of the Rig, Sama, Yajur and Atharva Vedas.
A janapada was a modern city with factories.
Janapadas were ancient territories where peoples settled.
Some janapadas grew into larger and stronger mahājanapadas.
The sabhā and samiti were kinds of musical instruments.
They were assemblies mentioned in Vedic texts.

quiz.q: What does 'janapada' mean?
options: The land where a people set foot and settled
quiz.explain: Jana means people; pada means foot. A janapada was a territory settled by a people.
quiz.mistake: Guesses the meaning without breaking the word into parts

quiz.q: Which is the oldest of the four Vedas?
quiz.explain: The Rigveda is the earliest Vedic text.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the order of the Vedas

quiz.q: How many Vedas are there?
quiz.explain: There are four Vedas: Rig, Sama, Yajur and Atharva.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the number of Vedas with the 16 mahājanapadas

quiz.q: What were the sabhā and the samiti?
quiz.explain: Vedic texts mention these gatherings where people discussed important matters.
quiz.mistake: Does not know these were assemblies

quiz.q: A 'jana' was:
quiz.explain: A jana was a group of people, a clan or tribe.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up jana with janapada

quiz.q: After the decline of the Harappan cities, people in northern India lived mostly in:
quiz.explain: For many centuries, life was mainly village-based before new cities rose again.
quiz.mistake: Thinks cities continued without a break

quiz.q: How did some janapadas become mahājanapadas?
options: By growing in land, people and wealth
quiz.explain: Stronger janapadas expanded and became 'great janapadas'.
quiz.mistake: Thinks 'maha' was just a title with no change in size or power

quiz.q: Why are the Vedas useful to historians?
options: They give exact dates of every king
They tell us about the life and beliefs of the people who composed them
quiz.explain: The Vedas are a window into the ideas, prayers and society of their time.
quiz.mistake: Expects ancient texts to be like modern record books

teach.ask: Gappu found the word 'janapada' in a book. Explain what it means and how janapadas began.
teach.praise: Janapada means land where people settled. And some grew into big ones!
teach.nudge: Close! What does 'jana' mean, and what does 'pada' mean?

learn.hook: Around 2,600 years ago, sixteen 'great janapadas' stretched across northern India, from Gandhara to Anga.
points: By about the 6th century BCE, there were sixteen mahājanapadas ('great janapadas'). Buddhist and Jain texts list them, though their lists differ slightly.
Examples with their capitals: Magadha (Rājagṛiha), Kosala (Shrāvastī), Avanti (Ujjayinī), Vatsa (Kaushāmbī), Gandhāra (Takshashilā), Kāshī (Vārāṇasī), Anga (Champā) and Vajji (Vaishālī).
Many mahājanapadas were ruled by kings. Some, like the Vajji and the Malla, were gaṇas or saṅghas, where power was shared by a group, and decisions were discussed in assemblies.
Mahājanapadas had capital cities, often protected by strong walls and moats, and collected taxes to pay for armies and officials.
They often fought one another for land and power. In time, Magadha became the most powerful.

example.q: A mahājanapada was ruled by an assembly of many leaders who discussed and decided matters together. Was it a monarchy?
steps: In a monarchy, one king rules and the throne usually passes in the family.
Here power was shared by a group in an assembly.
This matches a gaṇa or saṅgha.
example.answer: No. It was a gaṇa or saṅgha, where power was shared by a group.

learn.reallife: Ujjain (Ujjayinī), Varanasi and Patna (Pāṭaliputra) are still busy cities today, showing how old some Indian cities are.

quiz.q: How many mahājanapadas are named in the old Buddhist and Jain lists?
quiz.explain: The texts list sixteen great janapadas.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the number with other famous numbers

quiz.q: What was the capital of Magadha before Pāṭaliputra?
quiz.explain: Rājagṛiha (modern Rajgir in Bihar) was Magadha's early capital.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the capitals of different mahājanapadas

quiz.q: Vaishālī was the capital of which mahājanapada?
quiz.explain: Vaishālī was the centre of the Vajji, a well-known gaṇa or saṅgha.
quiz.mistake: Does not link Vaishālī with the Vajji

quiz.q: In a gaṇa or saṅgha, power was held by:
options: One king whose son always ruled after him
A group, with decisions discussed in assemblies
quiz.explain: Gaṇas were ruled collectively; many leaders met in assemblies.
quiz.mistake: Thinks all ancient states were monarchies

quiz.q: Ujjayinī was the capital of:
quiz.explain: Ujjayinī, today's Ujjain in Madhya Pradesh, was the capital of Avanti.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up Avanti and Vatsa

quiz.q: Why did mahājanapadas collect taxes?
options: To pay for armies, officials and walls
quiz.explain: Kings and councils needed wealth to keep armies, build forts and pay officials.
quiz.mistake: Does not see why rulers needed money

quiz.q: Which mahājanapada finally became the most powerful?
quiz.explain: Magadha, in present-day Bihar, grew strongest and later became the centre of empires.
quiz.mistake: Picks a smaller mahājanapada

quiz.q: Takshashilā, a famous centre of learning, was the capital of:
quiz.explain: Takshashilā was in Gandhāra in the north-west.
quiz.mistake: Does not link Takshashilā with the north-west

teach.ask: Gappu asks: what were the mahājanapadas, and how were they ruled?
teach.praise: Sixteen great states, some with kings and some ruled by assemblies. That's a lot of history!
teach.nudge: You named them, but were they all ruled the same way?

learn.hook: After a long gap following the Harappan age, cities appeared again in the Ganga plains, buzzing with traders, craftspeople and markets.
points: From about the 6th century BCE, new cities grew in the Ganga plains. Historians often call this the 'second urbanisation'; the Harappan cities were the first.
Iron tools like axes and ploughs helped people clear forests and grow more food. Extra food could feed people in cities who did not farm.
Cities like Rājagṛiha, Shrāvastī, Kaushāmbī, Vārāṇasī and Ujjayinī had fortification walls and moats, markets and crafts workshops.
Trade grew. Punch-marked coins, mostly of silver, were used to buy and sell. A shiny pottery called Northern Black Polished Ware is found at many of these sites.
Craftspeople and traders formed groups called shreṇīs (guilds). This was also the age of the Buddha and Mahāvīra.

example.q: Why did the use of iron tools help cities to grow?
steps: Iron axes cleared thick forests of the Ganga plains more easily.
Iron ploughs helped farmers grow more grain.
More food meant some people could live in towns as traders, craftspeople and officials.
example.answer: Iron tools increased farm output, and extra food could support city people who did not farm.

learn.reallife: Today's traders' associations are a bit like the shreṇīs of ancient times, where people in the same craft or trade worked together.

games.title: How a city grew
items: Extra food fed people who did not farm
Traders and crafts grew in towns

quiz.q: The rise of cities in the Ganga plains from about the 6th century BCE is often called:
quiz.explain: The Harappan cities were India's first cities; the Ganga-plain cities came much later, so this is the second urbanisation.
quiz.mistake: Forgets that Harappan cities came first

quiz.q: Which metal's use helped clear forests and grow more food?
quiz.explain: Iron axes and ploughs made clearing and farming easier.
quiz.mistake: Picks a precious metal instead of a tool metal

quiz.q: What were punch-marked coins mostly made of?
quiz.explain: Early Indian punch-marked coins were mostly silver pieces stamped with symbols.
quiz.mistake: Thinks coins were made of the same metal as tools

quiz.q: Why did many early cities build walls and moats?
options: To store water for drinking only
quiz.explain: Fortifications defended the city's wealth and people from enemies.
quiz.mistake: Does not see the defensive purpose of walls

quiz.q: A shreṇī was:
options: A guild of craftspeople or traders
quiz.explain: Shreṇīs were associations of people in the same craft or trade.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up shreṇī with other new words

quiz.q: Northern Black Polished Ware is a kind of:
quiz.explain: This glossy black pottery is found at many sites of this period.
quiz.mistake: Thinks 'ware' means a weapon or tool

quiz.q: Which great teachers lived in the age of the early cities and mahājanapadas?
quiz.explain: The Buddha and Mahāvīra lived around the 6th–5th centuries BCE.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up figures from different periods

quiz.q: Why could cities support people who did not farm?
options: City people did not need food
Farmers grew extra food that could be traded
quiz.explain: Surplus food from villages fed traders, crafts workers and officials in towns.
quiz.mistake: Does not see the link between farm surplus and towns

teach.ask: Gappu wonders why cities came back after the Harappan age. Explain what helped the new cities grow.
teach.praise: Iron tools, more food, trade and coins! Cities need villages to feed them.
teach.nudge: Good! But where did the extra food for city people come from?
